title: Crusoe sells troubled Wyoming data center project to Google
content:
Crusoe, an eight-year-old, Denver-based data center developer recently valued at $30.9 billion, confirmed Friday it has sold an unfinished data center project in southeastern Wyoming to Google.
Google, which Crusoe had tried and failed to land as a customer for the project, is taking over the development after reportedly raising concerns about its cost and construction timeline under Crusoe’s management.
Crusoe initially announced the project last year with Blackstone-backed infrastructure company Tallgrass, planning to eventually scale it to 10 gigawatts of power capacity.
Google did not disclose how much it paid Crusoe for the unfinished project, bu it announced plans to invest $17 billion to develop the data center campus.
The deal highlights how difficult it can be for independent data center developers to deliver massive projects on time and within budget, given the challenges of securing equipment and power. Growing opposition from local communities can further complicate development.
Despite taking over the Wyoming facility, Google hasn’t walked away from working with Crusoe entirely. Crusoe is developing another data center for Google near Amarillo, Texas.
The deal to sell the site to Google was first reported by Bloomberg in June, but the Wyoming setback didn’t stop Crusoe from raising a $3.9 billion round in September.
Crusoe makes money by leasing data center space to customers that bring their own GPUs, by renting out its own GPUs, and by selling compute power used to run AI models, known as inference.
Crusoe’s largest projects serve some of the biggest names in AI. Its campus in Abilene, Texas, is being built in phases for Oracle and OpenAI, and the company is also constructing a separate 900-megawatt campus next door for Microsoft, with its first building expected to come online in mid-2027. Meta is also a customer, and Bloomberg reported that the trading firm Jane Street signed a $13 billion, five-year cloud deal with Crusoe.
Crusoe was founded by Chase Lochmiller, now its CEO, and Cully Cavness, who started it as a cryptocurrency-mining business powered by natural gas that would otherwise have been burned off. In September, alongside its $3.9 billion funding round, the company added three board members, including JB Straubel, the Redwood Materials founder and Tesla board member who invested in Crusoe in 2021. Crusoe later became the first customer of Straubel’s energy-storage business.

report.summary: Crusoe sold its unfinished Wyoming data center to Google, which plans a $17B campus, showing how hard it is for independent developers to deliver massive AI projects.
report.background: The AI boom has triggered a race to build gigawatt-scale data centers, but power availability, equipment shortages, construction delays, and local opposition are making projects harder to deliver. Crusoe, founded eight years ago as a natural-gas-powered crypto miner, evolved into a data center developer and GPU cloud provider valued at $30.9 billion. It announced the Wyoming project last year with Blackstone-backed Tallgrass, aiming to scale to 10 gigawatts. Google was the intended customer but reportedly grew concerned about cost and timeline under Crusoe. Google’s takeover, first reported in June, comes as hyperscalers seek control over their own AI infrastructure and as independent developers face growing execution risk.
key_points: Crusoe confirmed it sold the unfinished southeastern Wyoming data center project to Google for an undisclosed price. Google plans to invest $17 billion to develop the campus. Crusoe had tried to land Google as a customer but Google reportedly raised concerns about cost and construction timeline under Crusoe’s management.

Crusoe remains a major AI infrastructure player. It leases data center space, rents GPUs, and sells inference compute. Its Abilene, Texas, campus is being built for Oracle and OpenAI, it is constructing a 900-megawatt campus for Microsoft, and Meta is a customer. Jane Street reportedly signed a $13 billion, five-year cloud deal.

The sale highlights execution risk for independent data center developers. Securing power, equipment, and permits is difficult, and local opposition can delay projects. Even Crusoe, despite a $30.9 billion valuation and a $3.9 billion funding round in September, stumbled on Wyoming.

The relationship is not over: Crusoe is developing another data center for Google near Amarillo, Texas. The Wyoming setback did not stop Crusoe’s fundraising, suggesting investors still see strong demand for AI compute capacity.
The deal reflects a broader trend: hyperscalers like Google are taking over projects when timelines or costs slip, rather than relying on third-party developers for critical AI capacity.
report.impact: For the AI industry, the deal reinforces consolidation: hyperscalers with strong balance sheets and construction teams are better positioned to absorb delays and cost overruns. Independent developers may need more partnerships or become niche suppliers. For developers, Google’s $17 billion commitment signals more compute capacity is coming, but if projects slip, GPU and inference capacity could remain tight, affecting pricing and availability. For regular users, the buildout ultimately shapes access to AI products, but delays can mean higher costs or limited features. Local communities will also face bigger debates over power use, water, and land as hyperscalers directly control projects.
report.tools: To follow the space, watch Crusoe Cloud and Google Cloud AI infrastructure offerings, plus the Open Compute Project (OCP) for open data center designs. For power and grid context, Electricity Maps and GridStatus offer open data on carbon intensity and grid conditions. MLPerf benchmarks help compare AI compute performance. These are useful for tracking how data center buildouts translate into available AI capacity.
